To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
FDG uptake in the CWR22 xenografts was significantly lower in castrated than in noncastrated mice, and that the FDG uptake in PC3 xenografts is higher than in the CWA22 xenograft.

the FDG accumulation in androgen sensitive CWR-22 human prostate cancer xenograph implanted in castrates male mice was lower than that of androgen insensitive PC-3 human prostate cancer xenographs implanted in non-castrated mice, indicating that the androgen may be involved in the regulation of glucose metabolism of prostate tumors.

the glucose metabolism in human prostate cancer xenotransplants is modulated by castration, and that FDG uptake in androgen-sensitive and androgen-independent human prostate cancer xenografts is higher in castrated mice than in noncastrated mice, and higher in the androgen-independent xenograft than in the androgen-sensitive xenograft.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a novel approach to the study of the glucose metabolism of human prostate cancer mouse xenografts.

the study of the metabolic changes in human prostate cancer xenotransplants in mice in response to castration and with the development of a novel method of imaging androgen ablation in vivo using positron emission tomography.
the development and validation of noninvasive molecular imaging technologies for the detection, diagnosis, and treatment of cancer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
FDG PET is useful in the imaging assessment of response to androgens ablation therapy and the early prediction of androgen independence in men with metastasis prostate cancer.

the glucose metabolism in the androgen-dependent prostate cancer xenografted into noncastrated mice is higher than that in the xenografts in the castrates, and the glucose metabolism in androgen-independent tumors is higher than in the androgen-sensitive tumors.
the androgen-sensitive prostate cancer xenografted in the castrates has significantly less glucose metabolism in comparison to the androgen-sensitive xenografted in noncastrated mice.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
FDG PET can be used to assess the response of androgen-sensitive human prostate cancer xenotransplants to castration in mice.
FDG uptake in prostate cancer is modulable by androgen and that the androgen-independent prostate cancer has higher FDG uptake than the androgen-sensitive prostate cancer.
FDG PET can be a useful tool to evaluate response to androgen-ablation therapy in patients with metastatic prostate carcinoma.
The main takeaway from our work is that
FDG uptake is higher in PC-3 tumors than in CWR-22 tumors.
androgen deprivation therapy may reduce the glucose metabolism in the prostate cancer xenografted in castrated host.
the glucose metabolism in human prostate cancer xenograph is modulated by the host castration status and by the hormone sensitivity of the tumor.
